title: Automated Testing
description: Making a suite you can trust: advanced Karate, mutation, architecture, load and property-based tests.
resumo: Karate at scale: `karate-config.js` per environment, `callonce` for login, Scenario Outline, parallel runs.
Mutation testing (PIT) measures whether tests catch bugs; target the domain, incremental in CI.
ArchUnit turns architecture rules into tests; freeze legacy violations, fail on new ones.
Load tests with thresholds (p95, error rate) in a production-like environment — and watch the generator.
Property-based tests check invariants over generated inputs — never a copy of the implementation.
Pipeline: unit on push, integration (Failsafe `*IT`) and contracts on PR, E2E and load in staging.

subsections.subtitle: Advanced Karate: Configuration, Reuse and Data
subsections.formerSubtitle: Karate Avançado: Configuração, Reuso e Dados
subsections.description: Environments, reusable features, data-driven scenarios and parallel runs.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every feature file logs in by itself, the base URL is hard-coded, and the suite takes 20 minutes because it runs one scenario at a time.

**Concept:** in bigger projects, `karate-config.js` sets the URL and credentials for each environment, chosen with `-Dkarate.env`. Repeated steps, such as getting a token, live in their own `.feature` file and are called with `call` or `callonce` (once per feature file). `Scenario Outline` with `Examples` runs one scenario for many inputs. The Runner executes scenarios in parallel and writes reports to `target/karate-reports`.

**How it works:** each scenario creates its own data instead of relying on execution order — required for running in parallel.
examples.interview_question: How do you organize Karate tests to run against several environments without logging in for every scenario?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using `call` in the `Background` for the login. The Background runs before every scenario, so each scenario logs in again — slow, and it can hit the auth server's rate limit. `callonce` runs it once per feature file.
examples.code:
# WRONG: logs in before every scenario
Background:
  * def auth = call read('classpath:auth/token.feature')

# RIGHT
Background:
  * def auth = callonce read('classpath:auth/token.feature')

subsections.subtitle: Mutation Testing
subsections.description: Do your tests actually catch bugs?

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** coverage is 90%, and a bug that flips a `>` into `>=` still reaches production.

**Concept:** coverage shows a line ran, not that its result was checked — a test with no assertions covers everything. Mutation tools such as PIT change the code (swap `>` for `>=`, remove calls, invert conditions) and run the tests: if no test fails, the mutant "survived" and reveals a missing check. The mutation score is a much more honest measure of a suite.

**How it works:** with JUnit 5, PIT needs the `pitest-junit5-plugin` dependency to find the tests.
examples.interview_question: Why doesn't 100% coverage guarantee good tests?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Running PIT over the whole codebase on every pull request. Mutation testing runs the suite many times, and a full run can take hours. Target the business-rule packages, and use incremental analysis (`withHistory`) in CI.
examples.code:
# WRONG: every class, every PR
mvn org.pitest:pitest-maven:mutationCoverage

# RIGHT: the domain packages, incremental
mvn org.pitest:pitest-maven:mutationCoverage -DwithHistory -DtargetClasses=com.shop.orders.domain.*

subsections.subtitle: Architecture Tests
subsections.description: Dependency rules checked by the build.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the team agreed controllers never touch repositories, and six months later a dozen do.

**Concept:** ArchUnit expresses architecture rules as JUnit tests: controllers do not access repositories, the domain does not depend on Spring, there are no cycles between packages. When someone breaks a rule, CI fails — the architecture no longer depends only on memory and code review.

**How it works:** start with a few rules that matter, and add more as the team agrees on them.
examples.interview_question: How do you stop a layered architecture from degrading over time?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Adding a strict rule to a legacy codebase in one go. It fails with hundreds of existing violations, so the rule is disabled and forgotten. Freeze the current violations, and fail only on new ones.

subsections.subtitle: Load and Performance Tests
subsections.description: Validating capacity and SLOs before production.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** Black Friday is the first time the system sees 20 times its normal traffic.

**Concept:** track latency percentiles (p95, p99), throughput, error rate and resource use (CPU, memory, pool connections). A load test simulates the expected traffic; a stress test increases load until something breaks, to find the limit; a soak test holds the load for hours to reveal leaks. Run in an environment close to production, with pass criteria (thresholds), so the test can run in the pipeline.

**How it works:** k6 thresholds make the run fail when the SLO is not met, exactly like a failing unit test.
examples.interview_question: Which metrics do you track in load tests?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Generating the load from a laptop on Wi-Fi. The laptop's CPU or network saturates first, and the test measures the load generator, not the system. Run the generator close to the system, and watch its own CPU.
examples.code:
WRONG: k6 on a laptop over Wi-Fi -> "the API maxes out at 300 req/s"
       (the laptop was at 100% CPU)

RIGHT: k6 on a machine in the same network/region, its CPU monitored —
       or distributed k6 for higher loads

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the tests check five hand-picked examples, and the bug appears with an input nobody thought of — zero, a negative number, an empty string.

**Concept:** instead of choosing examples, you describe a property that must hold for any input, and the library (jqwik) generates hundreds of cases, including edge cases such as zero, negatives and empty strings. When it finds a failure, it shrinks the input to the smallest counterexample.

**How it works:** good properties: invariants ("a discount never makes the price negative"), round trips ("parse(format(x)) == x"), and comparisons with a simpler implementation.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A property that recomputes the expected value with the same formula as the code. If the formula is wrong, the test is wrong in the same way and always passes. Test invariants, not a copy of the implementation.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every push runs the whole suite — unit, integration, end-to-end, load — and feedback takes 40 minutes.

**Concept:** split by speed: unit tests run first, on every push (fail fast); integration tests with Testcontainers run next, through Maven's Failsafe plugin (`*IT` classes); contracts are verified before merging; load and end-to-end tests run in staging before promotion to production. Run in parallel, publish reports, and treat a broken main as the first priority.

**How it works:** `mvn test` runs only Surefire (`*Test`); `mvn verify` also runs Failsafe (`*IT`).
examples.code:
mvn test      # Surefire: *Test.java (unit, seconds)
mvn verify    # Failsafe: *IT.java (integration with Testcontainers, minutes)

Pipeline:
  push      -> unit tests + static analysis
  PR        -> + integration + contract verification
  main      -> build the image -> deploy to staging -> E2E + load
  approval  -> production
examples.interview_question: How do you organize test execution in a CI pipeline?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Naming integration tests `*IT` without configuring Failsafe. Surefire does not run `*IT` classes, and Failsafe is not active by default in a plain Maven project, so those tests silently never run — the build is green either way. Add the plugin, and check the test count in the report.
examples.code:
<!-- RIGHT: without this, *IT classes are never executed -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals><goal>integration-test</goal><goal>verify</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
